extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political economy; economists and economic historians
extracted.subtask_description: Classical political‑economy analysis of the causes of changes in money prices, real prices, wages, and the value of precious metals across time and markets, with historical examples (England, Europe, America).

rubrics_metrics.name: transportation_and_local_price_differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prices between markets tend to approach the better market, but transportation difficulties and distances prevent perfect equalization: 'If the countries are near, the difference will be smaller... every commodity must commonly be somewhat dearer in the country to which it is brought than in that from which it comes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that transport costs and ease of carriage cause goods to be dearer at the destination than the source; proximity reduces differences; quality and conversion (e.g., flour from corn) affect comparative prices (English corn dearer in Scotland in money terms but cheaper in proportion to quantity/quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: real_recompence_of_labour_regulated_by_economic_condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion between the real recompence of labour in different countries is naturally regulated, not by their actual wealth or poverty, but by their advancing, stationary, or declining condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that trends of improvement (demand for labour) rather than absolute wealth determine real wages; evidence cited includes frequency of emigration and comparative money wages (Scotland vs England, Europe vs China).

rubrics_metrics.name: precious_metals_value_varies_with_national_wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold and silver are of the greatest value among the richest, and of the least value among the poorest nations; among savages they are scarce of any value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States a tendency for precious metals to command higher real value in richer, more commercial countries and very little value in the poorest societies, linking money demand to degree of commercial activity and wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: local_demand_and_urban_price_premium
rubrics_metrics.description: In great towns, corn is always dearer than in remote parts of the country; this is the effect of the real dearness of corn (not the real cheapness of silver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that supplying large towns costs more for corn than for coin; thus necessities fetch higher prices in population centers because of higher transport and supply costs, not because money is cheaper there.

rubrics_metrics.name: corn_as_a_long_run_measure_of_value
rubrics_metrics.description: Corn, at distant periods of time, is a more accurate measure of value than either silver or, perhaps, any other commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical corn prices to infer changes in the real value of silver; when silver rose or fell markedly in money terms, corn often remained a steadier benchmark for real purchasing power over long periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: effects_of_export_bounties_on_domestic_prices
rubrics_metrics.description: The parliamentary bounty upon the exportation of corn raises the price of corn above what it naturally would be in the actual state of tillage; by encouraging exportation it hinders the abundance of one year from compensating the scarcity of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains both short‑term and long‑term effects: in plentiful years bounty causes extraordinary exportation that raises home prices; in scarce years bounty is often suspended but overall tends to keep domestic prices higher than natural levels given local tillage.

rubrics_metrics.name: debasement_of_coin_and_nominal_price_increase
rubrics_metrics.description: The nominal sum which constitutes the market price of every commodity is regulated by the quantity of silver actually contained in the coin; this nominal sum is necessarily higher when the coin is much debased by clipping and wearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical example of clipped silver in 1695 (circulating coin near 25% below standard) raising nominal prices; emphasizes that nominal price responds to actual metallic content rather than standard denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: discovery_of_american_mines_lowered_silver_value_relative_to_corn
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of the abundant mines of America seems to have been the sole cause of the diminution in the value of silver (1570–1640); silver sunk in its real value and corn rose in its nominal price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that increased supply of silver from American mines outpaced demand, reducing the metal's real purchasing power (requiring more silver to buy a given quantity of corn), with chronological price data given for English wheat.

rubrics_metrics.name: natural_price_of_a_mined_commodity_determined_by_production_costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Silver would sink 'till it fell to its natural price; or to what was just sufficient to pay, according to their natural rates, the wages of the labour, the profits of the stock, and the rent of the land' required to bring it from the mine to market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the natural price of bullion as the cost floor determined by wages, profits, and rent in mining and transport; mining rents/taxes (Spanish royal tax examples) affect how low market price can fall while mines remain worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: market_expansion_increases_demand_for_money_metals
rubrics_metrics.description: The market for the produce of the American silver mines has been growing: (1) Europe improved and expanded demand, (2) America became a new market, (3) the East Indies and increasing Asiatic trade took off silver — these enlargements increased demand and prevented silver's value from falling further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains three channels of increased demand that absorbed additional silver supply: rising European consumption, development of American and colonial markets (coin/plate demand), and augmented trade with East Indies and Asia (e.g., Acapulco trade).

rubrics_metrics.name: supply_shocks_and_seasonal_effects_on_prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden changes in the price of corn (high prices during a run of bad seasons) should be attributed to accidental variations of the seasons and other supply shocks (e.g., civil war) rather than to rapid changes in the real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical episodes (civil war discouraging tillage; consecutive bad seasons; Polish disorders affecting supply) to argue that abrupt multi‑year price swings are best explained by supply disruptions, which operate faster than monetary changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: contract_price_vs_market_price_for_agricultural_produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The grower’s (contract) price is generally lower than what is supposed to be the average market price because it saves the farmer the expense and trouble of marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes contract/grower prices from average market prices and notes this when interpreting historical price series (Gregory King's estimate of grower's price vs observed market prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: nominal_vs_real_price_and_wage_relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between nominal money prices and real prices measured by labour: e.g., money price of labour rose in Great Britain during the present century owing to increased demand for labour (real recompence rose), whereas in France day wages tracked the average price of wheat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that nominal wage rises may reflect higher real wages in a prospering country (Britain) or move with staple prices in other countries (France), illustrating how local labour markets and demand conditions shape real vs nominal outcomes.
